'''''BMC Biology''''' is an online [[Open access (publishing)|open access]] [[scientific journal]] that publishes original, [[peer-review]]ed research in all fields of [[biology]], together with opinion and comment articles.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://bmcbiol.biomedcentral.com/about|title=About|website=BMC Biology|access-date=27 Sep 2019}}</ref> The publication was established in 2003.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.doaj.org/doaj?func=issues&jId=41254&uiLanguage=en|title=BMC Biology|author=<!--Staff writer(s); no by-line.-->|work=[[Directory of Open Access Journals|DOAJ]]|publisher=[[Infrastructure Services for Open Access|IS4OA]]|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130627231455/http://doaj.org/doaj?func=issues&jId=41254&uiLanguage=en|archive-date=27 June 2013|access-date=22 Apr 2013}}</ref> The journal is part of a series of [[BMC journals]] published by the UK-based publisher [[BioMed Central]], owned by [[Springer Nature]]. The journal has an international editorial board of researchers<ref>{{cite web|url=https://bmcbiol.biomedcentral.com/about/editorial-board|title=Editorial Board|website=BMC Biology|access-date=27 Sep 2019}}</ref> and editorial offices in London and New York.

Since 2010 it has incorporated what was previously the separate ''[[Journal of Biology]]''.

Video abstracts associated with the BMC Biology articles are collected on the BMC [[YouTube]] Channel.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.youtube.com/user/BioMedCentral/featured|title=BMC|website=YouTube|access-date=27 Sep 2019}}</ref>

[[File:Atmospheric Transmission.svg|thumb|upright=1.35|Τhe absorption bands of Earth's atmosphere (grey colour) delimit its atmospheric windows (middle panel) and the effect they have on both downgoing [[Solar irradiance|solar radiation]] and upgoing [[thermal radiation]] emitted near the surface is shown in the top panel. The individual absorption spectra of major greenhouse gases plus Rayleigh scattering are shown in the lower panel.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.noaa.gov/jetstream/satellites/absorb |title=The Atmospheric Window |publisher=[[National Oceanographic and Atmospheric Administration]] |accessdate=28 October 2022}}</ref>]]

An '''atmospheric window''' is a [[spectral band|region]] of the [[electromagnetic spectrum]] that can pass through the [[atmosphere of Earth]]. The [[Optical window|optical]], [[Infrared window|infrared]] and [[Radio window|radio]] windows comprise the three main atmospheric windows.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Introduction to the Electromagnetic Spectrum {{!}} Science Mission Directorate|url=https://science.nasa.gov/ems/01_intro|access-date=2021-12-28|website=science.nasa.gov |date=10 August 2016 }}</ref> The windows provide direct channels for Earth's surface to receive electromagnetic energy from the Sun, and for [[thermal radiation]] from the surface to leave to space.<ref name=kiehl97>{{Cite journal |title=Earth's Annual Global Mean Energy Budget |last1=Kiehl|first1=J. T.|last2=Trenberth|first2=Kevin E. |journal=Bulletin of the American Meteorological Society|volume=78|issue=2|pages=197–208|date=1 February 1997 |doi=10.1175/1520-0477(1997)078<0197:eagmeb>2.0.co;2 |bibcode=1997BAMS...78..197K|doi-access=free}}</ref> Atmospheric windows are useful for [[Observational astronomy|astronomy]], [[remote sensing]], [[telecommunications]] and other science and technology applications.

In the study of the [[greenhouse effect]], the term ''atmospheric window'' may be limited to mean the ''[[infrared window]]'', which is the primary escape route for a fraction of the thermal radiation emitted near the surface.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Cotton |first1=William R. |title=Human impacts on weather and climate |last2=Pielke |first2=Roger A. |publisher=[[Cambridge University Press]] |year=2007 |isbn=978-0-521-84086-6 |location=Cambridge |pages=180 |language=English |oclc=466742997}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last1=Rohli |first1=Robert V |title=Climatology |last2=Vega |first2=Anthony J |publisher=[[Jones & Bartlett Learning]] |year=2012 |isbn=978-0-7637-9101-8 |location=Sudbury, MA |pages=287 |language=English |oclc=569552317}}</ref> In other fields of science and technology, such as [[radio astronomy]]<ref>{{Cite book |last=Burke |first=Bernard F. |title=An introduction to radio astronomy |publisher=[[Cambridge University Press]] |year=2019 |isbn=978-1-107-18941-6 |location=Cambridge |pages=5 |language=English |oclc=1199628889}}</ref> and [[remote sensing]],<ref>{{Cite book |last=Joseph |first=George |title=Fundamentals of remote sensing. |publisher=Universities Press, India |year=2005 |isbn=978-81-7371-535-8 |location=Hyderabad |pages=43 |language=English |oclc=474734434}}</ref> the term is used as a [[Hyponymy and hypernymy|hypernym]], covering the whole electromagnetic spectrum as in the present article.

'''Biology by Team''' (in German {{lang|de|Biologie im Team}}) is the first Austrian biology contest for upper secondary schools.

Students at upper secondary schools who are especially interested in biology can deepen their knowledge and broaden their competence in experimental biology within the framework of this contest.

Each year, a team of teachers choose modules of key themes on which students work in the form of a voluntary exercise. The evaluation focuses in particular on the practical work, and, since the school year 2004/05, also on teamwork. In April, a two-day closing competition takes place, in which six groups of students from participating schools are given various problems to solve. A jury (persons from the science and corporate communities) evaluate the results and how they are presented.

The concept was developed by a team of teachers in co-operation with the AHS (Academic Secondary Schools) - Department of the Pedagogical Institute in [[Carinthia (state)|Carinthia]].

Since 2008 it is situated at the Science departement of the [http://www.ph-kaernten.ac.at University College of Teacher Training Carinthia]. The first contest in the school year 2002/03 took place under the motto: ''Hell is loose in the ground under us''. Other themes included ''Beautiful but dangerous'', ''www-worldwide water 1 and 2'', ''Expedition forest'', ''Relationship boxes'', ''Mole's view'', ''Biological timetravel'', ''Biology at the University'', ''Ecce Homo'', ''Biodiversity,'' ''Death in tin cans'', ''Sex sells'', ''Without a trace'', ''Biologists see more'', ''Quo vadis biology?'', ''Biology without limits?,'' ''Diversity instead of simplicity,'' ''Grid square,'' ''Diversity instead of simplicity 0.2,'' ''www-worldwide water 3, '' ''I hear something you don't see, '' ''Ready to change?''. The motto for the year 2025/26 is '' Bio Heroes - living beings as superheroes''.

Till now the following schools were participating:

* BG/BRG Mössingerstraße [[Klagenfurt]]
* Ingeborg-Bachmann-Gymnasium, [[Klagenfurt]]
* BG/BRG St. Martinerstraße [[Villach]]
* BG/BRG Peraustraße [[Villach]]
* International school Carinthia, [[Velden am Wörther See|Velden]]
* Österreichisches Gymnasium [[Prague|Prag]]
* Europagymnasium [[Klagenfurt]]
* BRG Viktring [[Klagenfurt]]
* BORG Wolfsberg [[Wolfsberg, Carinthia|Wolfsberg]]
* Stiftsgymnasium St. Paul im Lavanttal [[St. Paul im Lavanttal]]

BIT was submitted for the [https://www.biologie-im-team.at/innovationspreis-urkund.pdf German Innovations-prize for Sustainable Education] and placed among the 13 best of all nominated projects. With these prerequisites the base concept of "Biology By Team" can be replicated for other science and instructional fields and could provide an important contribution for the improvement of the subject and team competence of youth.

In 2008, BIT, the only Austrian biology competition, enabled the first Austrian participation at the EUSO - [[European Union Science Olympiad]].

{{Short description|Physical process}}
[[File:Granular jamming.svg|thumb|right|284x284px|Jamming during discharge of granular material is due to arch formation (red spheres)]]
[[File:Jamming phase diagram.png|thumb|220x220px|The second-order jamming phase diagram as introduced by O'Hern et al. (2003), expanding on Liu and Nagel (1998) where φ is packing fraction, T is temperature, and Σ is shear stress<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2">{{Cite journal |last1=Liu |first1=Andrea J. |last2=Nagel |first2=Sidney R. |date=November 1998 |title=Jamming is not just cool any more |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/23819 |journal=Nature |language=en |volume=396 |issue=6706 |pages=21–22 |doi=10.1038/23819 |bibcode=1998Natur.396...21L |issn=1476-4687|url-access=subscription }}</ref>.]]
'''Jamming''' is the physical process by which the viscosity of some [[Mesoscopic physics|mesoscopic]] materials, such as [[granular material]]s, [[glass]]es, [[foam]]s, [[polymer]]s, [[emulsion]]s, and other [[complex fluid]]s, increases with increasing particle density.  The jamming transition has been proposed as a new type of [[phase transition]], a strongly idealized hard-sphere [[glass transition]], but very different from the formation of
[[crystalline solid]]s.<ref name="nat_phys">{{cite journal
    |last=Biroli
    |first=Giulio
    |date=April 2007
    |title=Jamming: A new kind of phase transition?
    |journal=[[Nature Physics]]
    |volume=3
    |pages=222–223
    |doi=10.1038/nphys580
    |url=http://www.nature.com/nphys/journal/v3/n4/full/nphys580.html
    |access-date=2008-03-28
|bibcode = 2007NatPh...3..222B
    |issue=4|url-access=subscription
    }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Charbonneau |first1=Patrick |last2=Kurchan |first2=Jorge |last3=Parisi |first3=Giorgio |last4=Urbani |first4=Pierfrancesco |last5=Zamponi |first5=Francesco |date=2017-03-31 |title=Glass and Jamming Transitions: From Exact Results to Finite-Dimensional Descriptions |url=https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-conmatphys-031016-025334 |journal=Annual Review of Condensed Matter Physics |language=en |volume=8 |issue= |pages=265–288 |doi=10.1146/annurev-conmatphys-031016-025334 |arxiv=1605.03008 |bibcode=2017ARCMP...8..265C |issn=1947-5454}}</ref>

While a glass transition occurs when the liquid state is cooled, the jamming transition happens when the density, or the packing fraction of the particles, is increased.  This crowding of the constituent particles prevents them from flowing under an applied stress and from exploring [[phase space]], thus making the aggregate material behave as a solid.  The system may be able to unjam if [[Packing density|volume fraction]] is decreased, or external stresses are applied such that they exceed the yield stress. This transition is interesting because it is [[Nonlinear system|nonlinear]] with respect to volume fraction.

The jamming [[phase diagram]] relates the jamming transition to inverse density, stress
and temperature.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2" /><ref name="nature">{{cite journal
    |last=Trappe
    |first=V.
    |date=14 June 2001
    |title=Jamming phase diagram for attractive particles
    |journal=[[Nature (journal)|Nature]]
    |volume=411
    |pages=772–775
    |doi=10.1038/35081021
    |url=http://www.nature.com/nature/journal/v411/n6839/full/411772a0.html
    |access-date=2008-03-28
    |pmid=11459050
    |issue=6839
|bibcode = 2001Natur.411..772T |s2cid=661556
 |display-authors=etal|url-access=subscription
    }}</ref>

The density at which systems jam is determined by many factors, including the shape of their components, the deformability of the particles, frictional interparticle forces, and the degree of [[dispersity]] of the system. The overall shape of the jamming manifold may depend on the particular system. For example, a particularly interesting feature of the jamming transition is the difference between attractive and repulsive particle systems. Whether the jamming surface diverges for high enough densities or low temperatures is uncertain.

Simulations of jammed systems study particle configurations leading to jamming in both static systems and systems under shear. Under [[shear stress]], the average cluster size may diverge after a finite amount of strain, leading to a jammed state. A particle configuration may exist in a jammed state with a stress required to "break" the force chains causing the jam.

The simplest realization of a static jammed system is a random [[sphere packing]] of frictionless soft spheres that are jammed together upon applying an external hydrostatic pressure to the packing. Right at the jamming transition, the applied pressure is zero and the [[shear modulus]] is also zero, which  coincides with the loss of rigidity and the unjamming of the system. Also, at the jamming point the system is isostatic. Above the jamming point, the applied pressure causes an increase of [[volume fraction]] by squeezing the soft spheres closer together, and thus creates additional contacts between neighboring spheres. This leads to an increase of the average number of contacts <math> z </math>. As shown in numerical simulations by Corey O'Hern and collaborators, the [[shear modulus]] {{mvar|G}} increases with increasing <math> z </math> following the law: <math>G \sim (z-2d)</math>, where {{mvar|d}} is the dimension of space.<ref name=":1">{{cite journal | last1 = O'Hern | first1 = C. S. | last2 = Silbert | first2 = L. E. | last3 = Liu | first3 = A. J. | last4 = Nagel | first4 = S. R. | year = 2003 | title = Jamming at zero temperature and zero applied stress: The epitome of disorder. | journal = Physical Review E | volume = 68 | issue = 1 Pt 1| article-number = 011306 | doi = 10.1103/PhysRevE.68.011306| pmid = 12935136 | arxiv = cond-mat/0304421 | bibcode = 2003PhRvE..68a1306O | doi-access = free }}</ref> A first-principles microscopic theory of elasticity developed by [[Alessio Zaccone]] and E. Scossa-Romano quantitatively explains this law in terms of two contributions: the first term is a bonding-type contribution, thus proportional to <math> z </math>, and related to particle displacements which exactly follow the applied shear [[deformation (mechanics)|deformation]]; the second (negative) term is due to internal relaxations needed to keep local [[mechanical equilibrium]] in a strained disordered environment, and thus proportional to the total number of degrees of freedom, hence the dependence on space dimension {{mvar|d}}.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Zaccone | first1 = A. | last2 = Scossa-Romano | first2 = E. | year = 2011 | title = Approximate analytical description of the nonaffine response of amorphous solids. | arxiv=1102.0162 | journal = Physical Review B | volume = 83 | issue = 18| article-number = 184205 | doi = 10.1103/PhysRevB.83.184205 | bibcode = 2011PhRvB..83r4205Z | s2cid = 119256092 }}</ref> This model is relevant for compressed emulsions, where the friction between particles is negligible. 
Another example of static jammed system is a sand pile, which is jammed under the force of gravity and no energy is being dissipated.

A high dimensional limit [[mean-field theory]] for jamming was obtained by [[Giorgio Parisi]] and Francesco Zamponi,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Parisi |first1=Giorgio |last2=Zamponi |first2=Francesco |date=2010-03-16 |title=Mean-field theory of hard sphere glasses and jamming |url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/RevModPhys.82.789 |journal=Reviews of Modern Physics |language=en |volume=82 |issue=1 |pages=789–845 |doi=10.1103/RevModPhys.82.789 |arxiv=0802.2180 |bibcode=2010RvMP...82..789P |issn=0034-6861}}</ref> where clustering density and jamming density <math>\phi</math> scales as: <math display="block"> \phi \sim \frac{d \log(d)}{2^d} </math>Near jamming from below<math>\left(\phi \to \phi_J^- \right)</math>, the pair correlation function delta peak scales as:

<math>g(r) \sim \frac{1}{\delta}f \left( \frac{r-1}{\delta}\right)\text{, where } \delta \equiv\phi_J - \phi \to 0</math>

However, the square-root singularity of <math>g(r)</math> as seen from simulations was not present. The full solution, including critical scaling, was shown by Charbonneau et al. in 2014.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Charbonneau |first1=Patrick |last2=Kurchan |first2=Jorge |last3=Parisi |first3=Giorgio |last4=Urbani |first4=Pierfrancesco |last5=Zamponi |first5=Francesco |date=2014-04-24 |title=Fractal free energy landscapes in structural glasses |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/ncomms4725 |journal=Nature Communications |language=en |volume=5 |issue=1 |article-number=3725 |doi=10.1038/ncomms4725  |doi-access=free|pmid=24759041 |arxiv=1404.6809 |bibcode=2014NatCo...5.3725C |issn=2041-1723}}</ref>

Systems which are consuming energy are also sometimes described as being jammed. An example is [[traffic jam]]s, where due to jamming the average velocity of cars on a road may drop sharply. Here the cars on a road may be thought of like a [[granular material]] or a [[non-Newtonian fluid]] that is being pumped through a tube. There under certain conditions the effective [[viscosity]] may rapidly increase, dramatically increasing the [[granular material]] or [[fluid]]s's resistance to flowing and so causing the velocity to drop or even come to a complete stop. In this analogy the cars are like the grains in a [[granular material]] and if they are dense enough (i.e., closely enough spaced along the road) then interactions between the cars (as they must avoid each other to avoid crashing) cause jamming. A simple model of this behavior is the [[Nagel-Schreckenberg model]].

The notion of jamming can also be considered from a biophysical perspective to characterize the arrest of cellular motion.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal| doi = 10.1016/j.ceb.2021.07.011| issn = 0955-0674| volume = 72| pages = 146–155| last1 = Lawson-Keister| first1 = Elizabeth| last2 = Manning| first2 = M. Lisa| title = Jamming and arrest of cell motion in biological tissues| journal = Current Opinion in Cell Biology| series = Cell Dynamics| access-date = 2024-07-11| date = 2021-10-01| pmid = 34461581| url = https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S095506742100096X| arxiv = 2102.11255}}</ref> Cell motility is of importance in many biological processes including tissue morphogenesis, wound healing, and cancer invasion.<ref>{{Cite journal| doi = 10.1038/s41556-020-0552-6| issn = 1476-4679| volume = 22| issue = 9| pages = 1103–1115| last1 = Ilina| first1 = Olga| last2 = Gritsenko| first2 = Pavlo G.| last3 = Syga| first3 = Simon| last4 = Lippoldt| first4 = Jürgen| last5 = La Porta| first5 = Caterina A. M.| last6 = Chepizhko| first6 = Oleksandr| last7 = Grosser| first7 = Steffen| last8 = Vullings| first8 = Manon| last9 = Bakker| first9 = Gert-Jan| last10 = Starruß| first10 = Jörn| last11 = Bult| first11 = Peter| last12 = Zapperi| first12 = Stefano| last13 = Käs| first13 = Josef A.| last14 = Deutsch| first14 = Andreas| last15 = Friedl| first15 = Peter| title = Cell–cell adhesion and 3D matrix confinement determine jamming transitions in breast cancer invasion| journal = Nature Cell Biology| date = 2020-08-24| pmid = 32839548| pmc = 7502685}}</ref> 
<ref>{{Cite journal| doi = 10.1016/j.bbagen.2014.03.020| issn = 0304-4165| volume = 1840| issue = 8| pages = 2386–2395| last1 = Haeger| first1 = Anna| last2 = Krause| first2 = Marina| last3 = Wolf| first3 = Katarina| last4 = Friedl| first4 = Peter| title = Cell jamming: Collective invasion of mesenchymal tumor cells imposed by tissue confinement| journal = Biochimica et Biophysica Acta (BBA) - General Subjects| series = Matrix-mediated cell behaviour and properties| access-date = 2024-07-12| date = 2014-08-01| pmid = 24721714| url = https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S030441651400124X| url-access = subscription}}</ref> Characterizing the mechanisms that result in these "jamming" and "unjamming" phenomena can yield a more nuanced view of tissue development and aid in identifying new targets for disease therapies.<ref name=":0" />
<ref>{{Cite journal| doi = 10.1016/j.cdev.2021.203727| issn = 2667-2901| volume = 168| article-number = 203727| last1 = Atia| first1 = Lior| last2 = Fredberg| first2 = Jeffrey J.| last3 = Gov| first3 = Nir S.| last4 = Pegoraro| first4 = Adrian F.| title = Are cell jamming and unjamming essential in tissue development?| journal = Cells & Development| series = Quantitative Cell and Developmental Biology| date = 2021-12-01| pmid = 34363993| pmc = 8935248}}</ref>
Identifying properties defining these cellular phase changes has been a topic of recent interest. Cell density-based jamming is analogous to particle jamming in physical science, as the viscosity of a group of cells, like a group of particles, will increase as cell density increases.  Other key parameters uniquely discussed for cell jamming include cell shape, cell-cell contact, and cell motion, studied in both embryonic organization<ref>{{Cite journal| doi = 10.15252/embj.2019102497| issn = 0261-4189| volume = 38| issue = 20| pages = –102497| last1 = Petridou| first1 = Nicoletta I| last2 = Heisenberg| first2 = Carl-Philipp| title = Tissue rheology in embryonic organization| journal = The EMBO Journal| date = 2019-10-15| pmid = 31512749| pmc = 6792012}}</ref> and asthma.<ref>{{Cite journal| doi = 10.1038/nmat4357| issn = 1476-1122| volume = 14| issue = 10| pages = 1040–1048| last1 = Park| first1 = Jin-Ah| last2 = Kim| first2 = Jae Hun| last3 = Bi| first3 = Dapeng| last4 = Mitchel| first4 = Jennifer A.| last5 = Qazvini| first5 = Nader Taheri| last6 = Tantisira| first6 = Kelan| last7 = Park| first7 = Chan Young| last8 = McGill| first8 = Maureen| last9 = Kim| first9 = Sae-Hoon| last10 = Gweon| first10 = Bomi| last11 = Notbohm| first11 = Jacob| last12 = Steward Jr| first12 = Robert| last13 = Burger| first13 = Stephanie| last14 = Randell| first14 = Scott H.| last15 = Kho| first15 = Alvin T.| last16 = Tambe| first16 = Dhananjay T.| last17 = Hardin| first17 = Corey| last18 = Shore| first18 = Stephanie A.| last19 = Israel| first19 = Elliot| last20 = Weitz| first20 = David A.| last21 = Tschumperlin| first21 = Daniel J.| last22 = Henske| first22 = Elizabeth P.| last23 = Weiss| first23 = Scott T.| last24 = Manning| first24 = M. Lisa| last25 = Butler| first25 = James P.| last26 = Drazen| first26 = Jeffrey M.| last27 = Fredberg| first27 = Jeffrey J.| title = Unjamming and cell shape in the asthmatic airway epithelium| journal = Nature Materials| date = 2015-08-03| pmid = 26237129| pmc = 4666305| bibcode = 2015NatMa..14.1040P}}</ref> These factors are closely related to each other. In one attempt to illustrate the mechanisms of cell jamming, Lawson-Keister et al. use three factors: a) density, b) geometric incompatibility, and c) fluctuations.<ref name=":0" /> Efforts of experimentally quantifying cellular viscoelastic phases include in-vivo injection of force-sensing [[ferrofluid]],<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Mongera |first1=Alessandro |last2=Rowghanian |first2=Payam |last3=Gustafson |first3=Hannah J. |last4=Shelton |first4=Elijah |last5=Kealhofer |first5=David A. |last6=Carn |first6=Emmet K. |last7=Serwane |first7=Friedhelm |last8=Lucio |first8=Adam A. |last9=Giammona |first9=James |last10=Campàs |first10=Otger |date=September 2018  |title=A fluid-to-solid jamming transition underlies vertebrate body axis elongation |journal=Nature |language=en |volume=561 |issue=7723 |pages=401–405 |doi=10.1038/s41586-018-0479-2 |issn=1476-4687 |pmc=6148385 |pmid=30185907 |bibcode=2018Natur.561..401M }}</ref> micropipette aspiration,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Petridou |first1=Nicoletta I. |last2=Corominas-Murtra |first2=Bernat |last3=Heisenberg |first3=Carl-Philipp |last4=Hannezo |first4=Edouard |date=April 2021  |title=Rigidity percolation uncovers a structural basis for embryonic tissue phase transitions |journal=Cell |volume=184 |issue=7 |pages=1914–1928.e19 |doi=10.1016/j.cell.2021.02.017 |issn=0092-8674 |pmc=8055543 |pmid=33730596}}</ref> and 3D digital image correlation of cellular displacement.<ref>Tomizawa, Yuji; Wali, Khadija H.; Surti, Manav; Suhail, Yasir; Kshitiz; Hoshino, Kazunori (2025). "Single-Cell Quantification of Viscoelastic Phase Transitions in 3D Tissues". ''Advanced Materials Technologies''. '''10''' (6): 2401302. https://doi.org/10.1002/admt.202401302</ref>

In recent years, jamming as a limiting case of the glassy transition, once an active area of research, has seen a petering of interest.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Simons Collaboration on Cracking the Glass Problem |url=https://scglass.uchicago.edu/ |access-date=2026-04-11 |language=en-US}}</ref>

'''Hungarian art''' stems from the period of the conquest of the [[Carpathian basin]] by the people of [[Árpád]] in the 9th century.  Prince Árpád also organized earlier people settled in the area.

[[File:CCF12262007 00003.jpg|thumb|upright|Mountains west of Las Vegas in the [[Mojave Desert]]]]
[[File:Valley in Nevada.jpg|alt=A landscape shot of a long, dry valley. The sky is partially clouded over but blue sky breaks through in patches. It is a showcase of Nevada's natural beauty.|thumb|right|A valley near [[Pyramid Lake (Nevada)|Pyramid Lake]]]]
[[File:Digital-elevation-map-nevada.gif|thumb|right|Topographic map of Nevada]]

The landlocked U.S. state of '''[[Nevada]]''' has a varied geography and is almost entirely within the [[Basin and Range Province]] and is broken up by many north–south mountain ranges. Most of these ranges have [[Endorheic basin|endorheic]] valleys between them.

{{Short description|none}}
<!-- "none" is preferred when the title is sufficiently descriptive; see [[WP:SDNONE]] -->
[[File:Crater Lake - panoramio.jpg|thumb|right|[[Crater Lake]]]]

Oregon is {{convert|295|mi|km|0}} north to south at longest distance, and {{convert|395|mi|km|0}} east to west. With an area of {{convert|98381|sqmi|km2}}, Oregon is slightly larger than the [[United Kingdom]]. It is the ninth largest state in the United States.<ref>[http://factfinder2.census.gov/bkmk/table/1.0/en/DEC/00_SF1/GCTPH1R.US01PR Population, Housing Units, Area, and Density (geographies ranked by total population).] U.S. Census Bureau. Retrieved March 11, 2013.</ref> Oregon's highest point is the summit of [[Mount Hood]], at {{convert|11249|ft|m|0}}, and its lowest point is the sea level of the Pacific Ocean along the Oregon Coast.<ref name=usgs>{{cite web |date = April 29, 2005 |url = https://egsc.usgs.gov/isb/pubs/booklets/elvadist/elvadist.html |title = Elevations and Distances in the United States |publisher = U.S. Geological Survey |access-date = November 7, 2006 |url-status=dead |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20111015012701/http://egsc.usgs.gov/isb/pubs/booklets/elvadist/elvadist.html |archive-date = October 15, 2011 }}</ref> Oregon's mean elevation is {{convert|3300|ft|m|0}}. [[Crater Lake National Park]], the state's only national park, is the site of the deepest lake in the United States at {{convert|1943|ft|m|0}}.<ref>{{cite web |title = Crater Lake National Park |publisher = [[U.S. National Park Service]] |url = https://www.nps.gov/crla/index.htm |access-date = November 22, 2006 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20150702015100/http://www.nps.gov/crla/index.htm |archive-date = July 2, 2015 |url-status = live }}</ref> Oregon claims the [[D River]] as the shortest river in the world,<ref name="driver">{{cite web |url = http://www.oregonstateparks.org/park_214.php |title = D River State Recreation Site |website = Oregon Parks and Recreation Department |access-date = May 11, 2007 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20070418091225/http://www.oregonstateparks.org/park_214.php |archive-date = April 18, 2007 |url-status = live }}</ref> though the state of Montana makes the same claim of its [[Roe River]].<ref name="roeriver">{{cite web |url = http://montanakids.com/db_engine/presentations/presentation.asp?pid=192 |title = World's Shortest River |website = Travel Montana |access-date = May 11, 2007 |url-status=dead |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20070702003456/http://montanakids.com/db_engine/presentations/presentation.asp?pid=192 |archive-date = July 2, 2007 |df = mdy-all }}</ref> Oregon is also home to [[Mill Ends Park]] (in Portland),<ref name="pp&r">{{cite web |url = http://www.portlandonline.com/parks/finder/index.cfm?PropertyID=265&action=ViewPark |title = Mill Ends Park |website = Portland Parks and Recreation |access-date = May 11, 2007 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20120515141102/http://www.portlandonline.com/parks/finder/index.cfm?PropertyID=265&action=ViewPark |archive-date = May 15, 2012 |url-status = live }}</ref> the smallest park in the world at {{convert|452|sqin|m2|2}}.

Oregon is split into eight geographical regions. In [[Western Oregon]]: [[Oregon Coast]] (west of the [[Oregon Coast Range|Coast Range]]), the [[Willamette Valley]], [[Rogue Valley]], [[Cascade Range]] and [[Klamath Mountains]]; and in [[Central Oregon|Central]] and [[Eastern Oregon]]: the [[Columbia Plateau]], the [[High Desert (Oregon)|High Desert]], and the [[Blue Mountains (ecoregion)|Blue Mountains]].

Oregon lies in two [[time zone]]s. Most of [[Malheur County, Oregon|Malheur County]] is in the [[Mountain Time Zone]], while the rest of the state lies in the [[Pacific Time Zone]].

{{Short description|none}} <!-- "none" is preferred when the title is sufficiently descriptive; see [[WP:SDNONE]] -->
{{Use American English|date=July 2026}}
[[File:Map of Kentucky NA (cropped).png|thumb|A map of Kentucky]]

[[Kentucky]] is situated in the [[Upland South]] region of the United States.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www2.census.gov/geo/pdfs/maps-data/maps/reference/us_regdiv.pdf|title=Census Regions and Divisions of the United States|date=June 17, 2016|publisher=United States Census Bureau|website=U.S. Census Bureau|access-date=December 18, 2023}}</ref> A significant portion of eastern Kentucky is part of [[Appalachia]].

Kentucky borders seven states, from the [[Midwestern United States|Midwest]] and the [[Southeastern United States|Southeast]]. [[West Virginia]] lies to the northeast, [[Virginia]] to the east, [[Tennessee]] to the south, [[Missouri]] to the west, [[Illinois]] to the northwest, and [[Indiana]] and [[Ohio]] to the north. Only Missouri and Tennessee, both of which border eight states, touch more.

Kentucky's northern border is formed by the [[Ohio River]] and its western border by the [[Mississippi River]]; however, the official border is based on the courses of the rivers as they existed when Kentucky became a state in 1792. For instance, northbound travelers on [[U.S. Route 41 in Kentucky|U.S. 41]] from Henderson, after crossing the Ohio River, will be in Kentucky for about {{convert|2|mi|km|spell=in}}. [[Ellis Park Racecourse|Ellis Park]], a thoroughbred racetrack, is located in this small piece of Kentucky. Waterworks Road is part of the only land border between Indiana and Kentucky.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.mapquest.com/maps?address=%5B1300-1699%5D+Waterworks+Rd&city=Evansville&state=IN&zipcode=47713 |title=Map of <nowiki>[</nowiki>1494–1557<nowiki>]</nowiki> Waterworks Rd Evansville, IN |access-date=January 1, 2009}}</ref>

Kentucky has a non-contiguous part known as [[Kentucky Bend]], at the far west corner of the state. It exists as an [[exclave]] surrounded completely by [[Missouri]] and [[Tennessee]], and is included in the boundaries of [[Fulton County, Kentucky|Fulton County]]. Road access to this small part of Kentucky on the Mississippi River (populated by 18 people {{as of|2010|lc=y}})<ref>{{cite journal |author= <!--Staff writer(s); no by-line.--> |date= October 1, 2013 |title= Exclaves |journal= Virginia Quarterly Review |volume= 89 |issue= 4 |pages= 22–23 |issn= 0042-675X }}</ref> requires a trip through Tennessee.

The epicenter of the [[1811–12 New Madrid earthquakes]] was near this area, causing the Mississippi River to flow backwards in some places. Though the series of quakes changed the area geologically and affected the small number of inhabitants of the area at the time, the Kentucky Bend is the result of a surveying error, not the New Madrid earthquake.<ref>{{cite web | title=Life on the Mississippi | publisher=[[Kentucky Educational Television]] | date=January 28, 2002 | url=http://www.ket.org/kentuckylife/800s/kylife804.html | access-date=November 29, 2006 | archive-date=February 13, 2007 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070213074544/http://www.ket.org/kentuckylife/800s/kylife804.html | url-status=dead }}</ref>

{{Short description|none}} <!-- "none" is preferred when the title is sufficiently descriptive; see [[WP:SDNONE]] -->
[[File:Idaho map counties.svg|thumb|right|The counties of Idaho]]
The [[U.S. state]] of [[Idaho]] borders six other U.S. states and one [[Canadian province]]. The states of [[Washington (state)|Washington]] and [[Oregon]] are to the west, [[Nevada]] and [[Utah]] are to the south, and [[Montana]] and [[Wyoming]] are to the east. Idaho also shares a short border with the Canadian province of [[British Columbia]] to the north.

{{Short description|none}} <!-- "none" is preferred when the title is sufficiently descriptive; see [[WP:SDNONE]] -->
[[File:Utah Counties.png|thumb|Utah county boundaries]]

The landlocked U.S. state of Utah is known for its natural diversity and is home to features ranging from arid deserts with [[sand dune]]s to thriving [[pine tree|pine]] forests in mountain valleys. It is a rugged and geographically diverse state at the convergence of three distinct geological regions: the [[Rocky Mountains]], the [[Great Basin]], and the [[Colorado Plateau]].

{{Short description|none}}
[[File:Arizona ref 2001.jpg|thumb|upright=1.75]]
[[File:Map of USA AZ.svg|thumb|upright=1.2|The location of Arizona in the United States]]

[[Arizona]] is a landlocked state situated in the [[Southwestern United States|southwestern region]] of the [[United States|United States of America]]. It has a vast and diverse geography famous for its deep canyons, high- and low-elevation deserts, numerous natural rock formations, and volcanic mountain ranges. Arizona shares land borders with [[Utah]] to the north, the [[Mexico|Mexican]] state of [[Sonora]] to the south, [[New Mexico]] to the east, and [[Nevada]] to the northwest, as well as water borders with [[California]] and the Mexican state of [[Baja California]] to the southwest along the [[Colorado River]]. Arizona is also one of the [[Four Corners]] states and is diagonally adjacent to [[Colorado]].

Arizona has a total area of {{convert|113998|sqmi|km2|0}}, making it the [[List of U.S. states and territories by area|sixth largest]] U.S. state.<ref name="2000 Census Summary">[https://www.census.gov/prod/cen2000/phc3-us-pt1.pdf Summary of 2000 Census] Table 17</ref> Of this area, just 0.3% consists of water, which makes Arizona the state with the second lowest percentage of water area (New Mexico is the lowest at 0.2%).<ref name="2000 Census Summary"/> Arizona spans about {{convert|335|mi|km|0}} at its widest and {{convert|390|mi|km|0}} at its longest, and has an average elevation of about {{convert|4000|ft|m}}.<ref name="arizonahandbook">Weir, Bill. [http://www.arizonahandbook.com/AZ_the_land.htm The Land], ''arizonahandbook.com''.</ref> The geographic center of Arizona is located in [[Yavapai County, Arizona|Yavapai County]], approximately {{convert|55|mi|km|0}} east-southeast of the city of [[Prescott, Arizona|Prescott]].

{{Short description|US State Geography}}
<!-- "none" is preferred when the title is sufficiently descriptive; see [[WP:SDNONE]] -->
[[File:Counties of Wyoming, July 24, 2025.png|thumb|right|Map of the counties and capital city of Wyoming]]
The U.S. state of '''Wyoming''' lies in the [[Mountain states|Mountain West]] subregion of the [[Western United States]] and has a varied geography. It is bordered by [[Montana]] to the north and northwest, [[South Dakota]] and [[Nebraska]] to the east, [[Idaho]] to the west, [[Utah]] to the southwest, and [[Colorado]] to the south. Wyoming is the least populous U.S. state<ref>{{Cite web|date=April 26, 2021|title=2020 Census|url=https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/decennial/2020/data/apportionment/apportionment-2020-table01.pdf|website=Census.gov|access-date=July 12, 2021|archive-date=April 26, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210426194028/https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/decennial/2020/data/apportionment/apportionment-2020-table01.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref> and has the second-lowest population density behind [[Alaska]].

Wyoming's western half is covered mostly by the ranges and rangelands of the [[Rocky Mountains]], while the eastern half of the state is high-elevation [[prairie]] called the [[High Plains (United States)|High Plains]]. It is drier and windier than the rest of the country, being split between [[Semi-arid climate|semi-arid]] and [[continental climate|continental]] climates with greater temperature extremes. Almost half of the land in Wyoming is owned by the [[Federal government of the United States|federal government]], generally protected for public uses. The state ranks 6th by area and fifth by proportion of a state's land owned by the federal government.<ref name="maineenvironment.org">[http://www.maineenvironment.org/documents/publiclandownership.pdf MainEnvironment.org] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170525081957/http://www.maineenvironment.org/documents/publiclandownership.pdf |date=May 25, 2017 }} Public Land Ownership by State, 1995 Main Environment.org</ref> Federal lands within Wyoming include two national parks ([[Grand Teton National Park|Grand Teton]] and [[Yellowstone National Park|Yellowstone]]), two national recreation areas, two national monuments, several national forests, historic sites, fish hatcheries, and wildlife refuges.

{{Short description|none}} <!-- "none" is preferred when the title is sufficiently descriptive; see [[WP:SDNONE]] -->
[[File:Montana Map.jpg|thumb|right|Map of Montana]]
{{Use mdy dates|date=June 2023}}
[[Montana]] is one of the eight [[Mountain States]], located in the north of the region known as the [[Western United States]]. It borders [[North Dakota]] and [[South Dakota]] to the east. [[Wyoming]] is to the south, [[Idaho]] is to the west and southwest, and the [[Provinces of Canada|Canadian provinces]] of [[British Columbia]], [[Alberta]], and [[Saskatchewan]] are to the north, making it the only state to border three Canadian provinces.

With an area of {{convert|147040|sqmi|km2}},<ref name=census>{{cite web|url=https://www.census.gov/prod/cen2010/cph-2-1.pdf|title=United States Summary: 2010, Population and Housing Unit Counts, 2010 Census of Population and Housing|publisher=[[United States Census Bureau]]|type=PDF|page=41 (Table 18)|date=September 2012|access-date=April 11, 2014}}</ref> Montana is slightly larger than [[Japan]]. It is the fourth-largest state in the United States after [[Alaska]], [[Texas]], and [[California]],{{sfn|Anderson|2012|p=4}} and the largest landlocked state.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Montana {{!}} Capital, Population, Climate, Map, & Facts|url=https://www.britannica.com/place/Montana-state|access-date=February 17, 2021|website=Encyclopedia Britannica}}</ref>

{{Short description|none}} <!-- "none" is preferred when the title is sufficiently descriptive; see [[WP:SDNONE]] -->
[[File:National-atlas-arkansas.PNG|thumb|right|250px|Physical and human geographic features of Arkansas]]
The '''geography of [[Arkansas]]''' varies widely. The state is covered by mountains, river valleys, forests, lakes, and bayous in addition to the [[List of cities in Arkansas|cities of Arkansas]]. [[Hot Springs National Park]] features bubbling springs of hot water, formerly sought across the country for their healing properties.<ref>{{cite web |title= Hot Springs National Park |publisher= [[National Park Service]] |date= February 14, 2012 |url= https://www.nps.gov/hosp/index.htm |access-date= February 18, 2012 }}</ref><ref>{{ cite journal |last=Bryan |first=Kirk |title= The Hot Water Supply of the Hot Springs, Arkansas |publisher= The University of Chicago Press |journal= [[The Journal of Geology]] |volume= 30 |issue=6 |date= August–September 1922 |pages= 425–449 |oclc= 30653669 |doi=10.1086/622931|bibcode=1922JG.....30..425B |doi-access=  }}</ref> [[Crowley's Ridge]] is a geological anomaly rising above the surrounding lowlands of the [[Mississippi embayment]].

The [[Buffalo National River]], as it flows through [[The Ozarks]] to the [[White River (Arkansas)|White River]], is a popular tourist attraction. It was designated the first national river in 1972 after years of conservation efforts in opposition to a [[United States Army Corps of Engineers]] plan to dam the river. The [[Arkansas River]] enters the state near [[Van Buren, Arkansas|Van Buren]] and flows southeast through [[Little Rock, Arkansas|Little Rock]] to empty into the [[Mississippi River]] near [[Arkansas Post]]. Most of the river serves barge traffic to [[Tulsa, Oklahoma]], as the [[McClellan–Kerr Arkansas River Navigation System]].<ref>{{cite web |title= What is the McClellan-Kerr Arkansas River Navigation System? |publisher= [[U.S. Army Corps of Engineers]] |date= April 26, 2010 |url= http://www.swl.usace.army.mil/navigation/mckarns.html |access-date= February 18, 2012 |url-status= dead |archive-url= https://archive.today/20120805153455/http://www.swl.usace.army.mil/navigation/mckarns.html |archive-date= August 5, 2012 }}</ref> Through south Arkansas, the [[Ouachita River]] and the [[Saline River (Ouachita River)|Saline River]] run roughly parallel to the Arkansas, and the major rivers in northeast Arkansas are the White River and [[St. Francis River]]. The [[Red River of the South|Red River]] runs through the southwest corner of the state.

Arkansas has many manmade lakes across the state, many are the basis for [[List of Arkansas state parks|state parks]], [[List of Arkansas Wildlife Management Areas|wildlife management areas]], or other recreation. [[Bull Shoals Lake]], [[DeGray Lake]], [[Lake Dardanelle]], [[Lake Ouachita]] all have state parks along their shores, and [[Beaver Lake (Arkansas)|Beaver Lake]], [[Table Rock Lake]], [[Greers Ferry Lake]], [[Lake Hamilton and Lake Catherine]] are also major recreation lakes in the state.<ref name="guide">{{ cite book |title= Arkansas State Parks Guide, 2011 |url= http://www.nxtbook.com/nxtbooks/aristotle/arkansasstateparks2011/ |publisher= [[Arkansas Department of Parks and Tourism]] |access-date= February 18, 2012 }}</ref>

[[The Ozarks]] is a broad term for many mountainous counties in northwest Arkansas. This region is usually referred to the Ozarks because the term Northwest Arkansas is the colloquial name for the [[Fayetteville–Springdale–Rogers Metropolitan Area]], including [[Benton County, Arkansas|Benton]], [[Madison County, Arkansas|Madison]], [[Washington County, Arkansas|Washington]] counties in Arkansas and [[McDonald County, Missouri]].<ref>{{ cite map |title= Metropolitan and Micropolitan Statistical Areas of the United States and Puerto Rico, December 2009 |date= August 31, 2010 |url= http://www2.census.gov/geo/maps/metroarea/us_wall/Dec_2009/cbsa_us_1209.pdf |format= PDF |publisher= [[United States Census Bureau]] Economics and Statistics Administration |cartography= Geography Division }}</ref> The Ozark, however, span from the Arkansas River in the south through north central Arkansas. The [[Boston Mountains]] subset contain highest peaks in the Ozarks.<ref>{{ cite journal |last= Purdue |first= A. H. |title= Physiography of the Boston Mountains, Arkansas |journal= Journal of Geology |volume= 9 |issue= 8 |date= November–December 1901 |pages= 694–701 |publisher= The University of Chicago Press |doi= 10.1086/620967 |bibcode= 1901JG......9..694P |s2cid= 129914010 |oclc=41344070 }}</ref>

{{Short description|none}} <!-- "none" is preferred when the title is sufficiently descriptive; see [[WP:SDNONE]] -->
{{Good article}}
[[File:Wisconsin ref 2001.jpg|thumb|upright=1.75|A general map of Wisconsin]]

[[Wisconsin]], a [[U.S. state|state]] in the [[Midwestern United States]], has a vast and diverse geography famous for its landforms created by glaciers during the [[Wisconsin glaciation]] 17,000 years ago. The state can be generally divided into five geographic regions—Lake Superior Lowland, Northern Highland, Central Plain, Eastern Ridges & Lowlands, and Western Upland. The southwestern part of the state, which was not covered by [[glacier]]s during the most recent ice age, is known as the [[Driftless Area]].<ref name="Spoolman (2018) p. 129">{{harvp|Spoolman|2018|p=129}}</ref> The Wisconsin glaciation formed the [[Dells of the Wisconsin River|Wisconsin Dells]], [[Devil's Lake (Wisconsin)|Devil's Lake]], and the [[Kettle Moraine]]. A number of areas are protected in the state, including [[Devil's Lake State Park (Wisconsin)|Devil's Lake State Park]], the [[Apostle Islands National Lakeshore]], and the [[Chequamegon–Nicolet National Forest]].

Wisconsin has a [[humid continental climate]] across the entire state, with four distinct [[Season|seasons]]. Temperatures typically range from a high of {{Convert|80|°F|°C}} in the summer months to a low of {{Convert|5|°F|°C}} in the winter months. The state is bounded by several rivers—the [[Mississippi River|Mississippi]], [[St. Croix River (Wisconsin–Minnesota)|St. Croix]], and [[Menominee River|Menominee]] rivers—and lakes [[Lake Michigan|Michigan]] and [[Lake Superior|Superior]]. Wisconsin has an average elevation of {{Convert|1050|ft|m}},<ref>{{Cite web|title=State Elevation Ranking (by mean elevation) from NETSTATE.COM|url=https://www.netstate.com/states/tables/state_elevation_mean.htm|access-date=2021-10-17|website=www.netstate.com}}</ref> and is the 23rd-largest in the country, with an area of {{Convert|65,496|sqmi|km2}}.

{{Short description|none}} <!-- "none" is preferred when the title is sufficiently descriptive; see [[WP:SDNONE]] -->
[[File:Michigan.svg|right|thumb|Michigan map, including territorial waters.]]

[[Michigan]] consists of two peninsulas surrounded primarily by four of the [[Great Lakes]] and a variety of nearby islands. The [[Upper Peninsula of Michigan|Upper Peninsula]] is bounded on the southwest by [[Wisconsin]], and the [[Lower Peninsula of Michigan|Lower Peninsula]] is bounded on the south by [[Indiana]] and [[Ohio]]. Both land masses are also separated from the Canadian province of [[Ontario]] by waterways of the Great Lakes, and from each other by the [[Straits of Mackinac]]. Because its land is largely surrounded by the Great Lakes, which flow into the [[Saint Lawrence River]], Michigan is the only U.S. state whose streams and rivers are almost entirely within the Great Lakes-St. Lawrence watershed. Besides the island state of [[Hawaii]], Michigan is the only state whose area is largely composed of non-contiguous parts, and before the completion of the [[Mackinac Bridge]] was entirely bifurcated between its upper and lower peninsulas. 

Michigan's [[territorial waters]] include roughly half each of [[Lake Superior]], [[Lake Michigan]], and [[Lake Huron]], and smaller areas of [[Lake St. Clair]] and [[Lake Erie]]. It includes an estimated 11,000 inland lakes.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.canr.msu.edu/michiganlakes/faq|title=FAQ|website=Michigan Inland Lakes Partnership|language=en|access-date=2020-03-05}}</ref> It encompasses {{convert|58110|sqmi|km2}} of land, {{convert|38575|sqmi|km2}} of Great Lakes waters, and {{convert|1305|sqmi|km2}} of inland waters. Its territorial waters are second in area only to those of [[Alaska]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.infoplease.com/ipa/A0108355.html|title=Land and Water Area of States, 2000}}</ref> At a total area of {{convert|97990|sqmi|km2}} – including those territorial waters – Michigan is the largest state east of the [[Mississippi River]], and the eleventh largest state overall. More than half of the state's land area – {{convert|30156|sqmi|km2}} – is still [[forest]].

The state lies roughly between 41° and 49° north latitude, and between 82° and 91° west longitude.

{{Short description|Astronomy in Ancient Egypt}}
[[File:Astronomical Ceiling, Tomb of Senenmut MET DT207429.jpg|thumb|right|200px|[[Astronomical ceiling of Senenmut's Tomb|Astronomical ceiling]] from the [[TT71|Tomb of Senenmut]] ([[Eighteenth Dynasty of Egypt|XVIII Dynasty]], circa 1479–1458 BCE), discovered in [[Thebes, Egypt|Thebes]], [[Upper Egypt]]; facsimile preserved in the [[Metropolitan Museum of Art]].<ref>Full version at [http://www.metmuseum.org/Collections/search-the-collections/100000870#fullscreen Met Museum]</ref>]]
[[File:Goddess Nut 1.JPG|thumb|right|200px|The [[sky goddess]] [[Nut (goddess)|Nut]] and human figures representing stars and constellations from the star chart in the tomb of [[Ramses VI]], c. 1140 BC]]

'''Egyptian astronomy''' started in [[prehistory|prehistoric]] times, in the [[Prehistoric Egypt|Predynastic Period]]. In the 5th millennium BCE, the stone circles at [[Nabta Playa]] may have made use of astronomical alignments. By the time the historical [[Ancient Egypt|Dynastic Period]] began in the 3rd millennium BCE, the 365 day period of the [[Egyptian calendar]] was already in use, and the observation of [[star]]s was important in determining the annual flooding of the [[Nile]].

The [[Egyptian pyramids]] were carefully aligned towards the [[pole star]],<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Stargazers of Ancient Egypt {{!}} Science and Technology {{!}} BBC World Service |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/worldservice/sci_tech/highlights/001116_pyramids.shtml |access-date=2026-09-12 |website=www.bbc.co.uk}}</ref> and the temple of [[Amun|Amun-Re]] at [[Karnak]] was aligned on the rising of the [[winter solstice|midwinter]] Sun.{{citation needed|date=September 2024}} [[Astronomy]] played a considerable part in fixing the dates of [[religious festival]]s and determining the hours of night, and temple [[astrology|astrologers]] were especially adept at watching the stars and observing the [[conjunction (astronomy)|conjunctions]] and risings of the [[Sun]], [[Moon]], and [[planet]]s, as well as the [[lunar phase]]s.

In [[Ptolemaic Kingdom|Ptolemaic Egypt]], the Egyptian tradition merged with [[Greek astronomy]] and [[Babylonian astronomy]], with the city of [[Alexandria]] in [[Lower Egypt]] becoming the centre of scientific activity across the [[Hellenistic world]]. [[Egypt (Roman province)|Roman Egypt]] produced the greatest astronomer of the era, [[Ptolemy]] (90–168 CE). His works on astronomy, including the [[Almagest]], became the most influential books in the history of Western astronomy. In [[Egypt in the Middle Ages|Medieval Egypt]], the region came to be [[Egypt in the Middle Ages|dominated by Arabic culture]] and [[astronomy in medieval Islam|Islamic astronomy]].

The astronomer [[Ibn Yunus]] (c. 950–1009) observed the [[position of the Sun|Sun's position]] for many years using a large [[astrolabe]], and his observations on [[eclipse]]s were still used centuries later. In 1006, [[Ali ibn Ridwan]] observed the [[SN 1006]], a [[supernova]] regarded as the brightest stellar event in [[recorded history]], and left the most detailed description of it. In the 14th century, [[Najm al-Din al-Misri]] wrote a treatise describing over 100 different types of scientific and astronomical instruments, many of which he invented himself.
